title: Methodus generalior numeros quosvis satis grandes perscrutandi utrum sint primi necne?

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E719 tests whether N = 1848a² + b² is prime by checking that it has only one representation in the form 1848a² + b². 1848 is one of Euler's idoneal numbers (numeri idonei). The worked example is a = 100, b = 197, N = 18518809. Writing the second number as y = 21z + 197 and splitting by congruence classes gives four cases. Each case becomes a single-variable condition 10000 − S(s) = x², where S is a quadratic in s with leading coefficient 231/2. Euler checks each condition by subtracting successive first differences, which grow by the constant second difference 231, from 10000, or from 10000 + |S(0)| when S(0) < 0. He stops when the remainder is smaller than the next difference and checks whether any remainder is a perfect square.

This page finishes case 2 (§68). Here S = ½s(231s ± 197). The differences are 214, 445, 676, … in one column and 17, 248, 479, … in the other.
- First column remainders: 9786, 9341, 8665, 7758, 6620, 5251, 3651, 1820.
- Second column remainders: 9983, 9735, 9256, 8546, 7605, 6433, 5030, 3396, 1531.
- None of these is a square. The only square is 10000 itself (s = 0), which reproduces the known representation (100, 197).

Case 3 (§69): the condition is 10000 − ½(7s − 591)(33s − 2758) = x². Substituting s = 84 + t gives ½(7t − 3)(33t + 14).
- Values: S(0) = −21; S(1) = 94, S(2) = 440, S(3) = 1017; S(−1) = 95, S(−2) = 442, S(−3) = 1020.
- Differences: 115, 346, 577, … and 116, 347, 578, …, both rising by 231.
- Subtracting from 10021, the left column gives 9906, 9560, 8983, 8175, 7136, 5866, 4365, 2633, 670.
- The right column gives 9905, 9558, 8980, 8171, 7131, 5860, 4358, 2625, 661.
- None is a square, so this case also yields no second representation.

The page serves Euler's conclusion in §71 that 18518809 is prime, because its representation by 1848a² + b² is unique.
errors: In the case-3 left column the print reads 8075 and 7036. The correct values are 8983 − 808 = 8175 and 8175 − 1039 = 7136. The next printed value, 5866 = 7136 − 1270, is correct, so these are typesetting slips only. Neither 8175 nor 7136 is a square, so the conclusion is unaffected.
All other subtractions and table values on the page check out. The substitutions are correct: 7·84 − 591 = −3 and 33·84 − 2758 = 14.

ideas.what: Primality test by showing that N has a unique representation by the form x² + 1848y², using an idoneal number
ideas.modern_name: Euler's idoneal-number primality criterion; uniqueness of representation by genus-one forms
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1778 onward); treated by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae §303 and §329ff
ideas.where_published: E498, E708, E715, E719 and related papers in Nova Acta; Euler's correspondence with Beguelin

ideas.what: Searching for squares of the form C − Q(t), with Q quadratic, by successive subtraction of first differences with constant second difference
ideas.modern_name: Finite-difference sieve for a quadratic Diophantine condition (Fermat-style difference method)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Fermat and Euler; a standard technique
ideas.where_published: Used throughout Euler's factorization papers, e.g. E369 and E699

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine continuation of Euler's well-known worked example that 18518809 is prime via the idoneal number 1848. The only finding is two printing slips that do not affect the result.
transcription_corrections: The transcription's '8075 [?]' matches the print, but the correct value is 8175; the scan shows the typo as printed.
The transcription's '7036 [?]' matches the print, but the correct value is 7136; this is also a typo in the print.
'9560' in the left column of case 3 is printed '956a'-like in the scan; it is 9560.
